Twice as many electrons are emitted, each with the same maximum kinetic energy
The threshold frequency of the metal halves

questions.feedback: That trap reading is the one to unlearn: Brighter light ejects faster electrons. Reteach point: Brightness means more photons, not stronger ones: a dim violet beam ejects faster electrons than a bright red one.
questions.prompt: A beam of light on a metal is made twice as bright at the same frequency, and electrons were already being emitted. What changes?

questions.feedback: The stopping potential turns the fastest electrons back: e V_s = KE_max, so divide the maximum kinetic energy by the electron charge. 4.65 / 1.60 = 2.9 V - if you used a brighter beam you would get the same 2.9 V, just more current to stop.
questions.prompt: For the ultraviolet light and metal of the worked example (KE_max = 4.65 x 10^-19 J), calculate the stopping potential. (e = 1.60 x 10^-19 C)

choices.text: More electrons are emitted, at the same maximum kinetic energy
Electrons are emitted with a greater maximum kinetic energy, because each photon now carries more energy
No electrons are emitted until the intensity also increases

questions.feedback: Frequency writes the cheque: raise f and each photon carries more energy h f, so after paying the same work function the electrons keep more as kinetic energy. Intensity, not frequency, is the knob for how many electrons come out.
questions.prompt: The frequency of the light on a metal plate is increased, staying above the threshold frequency. What happens to the emitted electrons?

questions.answer: The work function W is the minimum energy an electron needs to escape the metal surface. The threshold frequency f0 = W / h is the lowest frequency whose photons each carry at least W; below f0 no electrons are emitted, however bright the light.
questions.feedback: Both definitions live in scene s2: the work function is the exit fee, and the threshold frequency is where one photon exactly covers it, h f0 = W.
questions.prompt: Define the work function of a metal and the threshold frequency of light for that metal.
